strengths: Part-centric spatial modeling is conceptually sound and timely: shifting from coarse object-level scene graphs to Part-centric Assembly Graphs (PAGs) explicitly resolves ambiguities in spatial prepositions (e.g., specific supporting/contacting surfaces).

The construction of PARSE-10K is a valuable resource contribution, providing 10,000 3D indoor scenes with an average of 49.9 objects per scene, part-level segmentations, and contact annotations validated via physics simulation.

The coarse-to-fine Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver is well-formulated, leveraging the DAG hierarchy of support relations to turn a global combinatorial placement problem into sequential, constrained pose sampling.

The utility of the dataset is demonstrated across two distinct tasks: fine-tuning vision-language models for spatial reasoning/scene graph generation and conditioning diffusion models for 3D scene synthesis.
weaknesses: Fairness and depth of VLM benchmarking: In Table 2, 'Ours' (Qwen3-VL fine-tuned on PARSE-10K) is directly compared against generalist models (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, zero-shot Qwen3-VL) on synthesized evaluation tasks derived from the same distribution. A breakdown of performance specifically on real images (such as the mentioned COCO subset or standard 3D/2D SGG benchmarks) is needed to show whether the learned part-level grounding genuinely transfers outside synthetic renderings.

Evaluation of 3D scene generation lacks standard objective metrics: The evaluation in Section 5.2 relies entirely on qualitative visual comparisons and a user study of 20 participants across 12 scenes. Standard quantitative metrics in 3D layout synthesis (e.g., collision rate / intersection volume, out-of-boundary rate, physical stability percentage under simulation, FID/KLD of layout distributions) should be reported.

Unfair baseline comparison in scene generation: The baseline InstructScene is trained on 3D-FRONT (which averages only ~6.9 objects per room), whereas the proposed model is trained on PARSE-10K (~49.9 objects per room). The higher object count and complexity perceived in the user study are largely an artifact of the training data distributions rather than purely the methodological advantage of PAG conditioning.

Clarity regarding PAG generation from real images: The paper mentions extracting layout priors from real images to build PAGs, but provides minimal detail on how these priors are extracted, how much human curation was required, and how scalable this pipeline is to arbitrary novel scenes.

strengths: Well-motivated formulation: Moving from coarse object-level spatial relations to part-aware relational modeling addresses fundamental ambiguities in physical support, alignment, and contact, bridging high-level linguistic relations and low-level physical constraints.

Tractable hierarchical solver: Formulating the Part-centric Assembly Graph (PAG) as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) allows decomposing the complex global scene constraint satisfaction problem into a sequential, coarse-to-fine localization and alignment process followed by physics simulation.

Valuable dataset contribution: PARSE-10K provides 10,000 indoor scenes with high object density (~50 objects per scene), 17k+ part-segmented 3D assets, and dense part-to-part contact annotations, serving as a rich asset for both 3D scene understanding and generation.
Comprehensive downstream exploration: The utility of PARSE is demonstrated across two distinct tasks: 2D vision-language spatial reasoning / scene graph generation and 3D scene layout synthesis.
weaknesses: Lack of standard objective quantitative metrics for 3D scene generation: The scene generation evaluation in Section 5.2 relies almost entirely on a 20-person user study over only 12 scenes. Standard geometric and physical metrics (e.g., collision rate, physical stability/floating rate after simulation, boundary violations, and graph relation satisfaction accuracy) are missing.

Evaluation domain bias in VLM experiments: In Table 2, the fine-tuned Qwen3-VL is evaluated on test tasks derived directly from the PARSE-10K rendering pipeline against general-purpose zero-shot VLMs. Although the text notes that some real COCO images were included in the test set, no separate breakdown between synthetic in-domain data and real-world out-of-domain images is provided, making it difficult to assess true generalization versus distribution memorization.

Ambiguity in initial PAG construction: The paper notes that PAGs are constructed by 'extracting layout priors from real images', but later admits in the limitations that PAG construction is 'partially manual and sensitive to canonical poses.' The exact pipeline, level of human annotation required, and scalability of PAG extraction from unannotated images or text prompts remain underspecified.

Geometric limitations of planar surface alignment: The part alignment solver assumes canonical oriented planar faces (top, bottom, front, back, left, right). This restricts handling irregular, highly curved, or non-axis-aligned contact geometries (e.g., complex nesting or tightly fitted oblique surfaces).

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and important shortcoming in 3D scene modeling and scene graph representations: conventional object-level scene graphs treat objects as indivisible bounding volumes, failing to capture the fine-grained part-to-part contacts, supports, and alignments required for physically plausible spatial modeling.

The Part-centric Assembly Graph (PAG) formulation as a two-level Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is conceptually clean and computationally convenient, allowing sequential coarse-to-fine constraint propagation and pose sampling.

The resulting PARSE-10K dataset is large (10,000 scenes across 17 room types) and exhibits high object density (averaging ~50 objects/scene) with part-level segmentation and explicit contact graphs, which could be a useful resource for spatial reasoning and layout synthesis.
The manuscript is clearly structured, with informative visual illustrations (e.g., Figures 2 and 3) explaining the hierarchy and solver stages.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison in Table 2: The fine-tuned Qwen3-VL ('Ours') is evaluated against generalist zero-shot/few-shot models (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, etc.) primarily on rendered synthetic images from the PARSE-10K distribution. Because the test evaluation relies on the specific taxonomy, part segmentation definitions, and relational schema introduced in this dataset, evaluating in-domain fine-tuned models against off-the-shelf generalist VLMs heavily skews the results. The paper mentions adding a small number of manually annotated COCO images, but fails to report separate quantitative results or ablation on real-world data.

Confounded comparison in 3D scene generation (Table 3 and Figure 6): The baseline (InstructScene) is trained on 3D-FRONT (which has an average of only ~7 objects per scene), whereas the proposed model is trained on PARSE-10K (~50 objects per scene). In the user study evaluating complexity, realism, and contact fidelity, comparing models trained on two fundamentally different datasets conflates dataset statistics (density and diversity) with the architectural and relational merits of PAG conditioning.

Lack of technical clarity on the PAG construction pipeline: The manuscript asserts that PAGs are extracted from 'real-image layout priors' to construct the 10,000 scenes, but Section 4 provides almost no technical detail on how this image-to-PAG extraction is performed (e.g., whether it relies on automated heuristics, human annotation, or LLM/VLM parsing). The limitations section additionally mentions that 'PAG construction [is] partially manual,' leaving the actual scalability and automated reproducibility of the pipeline ambiguous.

Limited novelty and flexibility in the geometric solver: The Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver is primarily an assembly of classical procedural heuristics (planar support rejection, canonical surface coplanarity constraints, ray-casting enclosure tests, and settling via Sapien rigid-body physics). As acknowledged in Section 6, the reliance on canonical oriented faces (top, bottom, front, etc.) restricts contacts to near-parallel planar surfaces and struggles with non-axis-aligned, oblique, or non-rigid physical interactions.

strengths: Compelling motivation and formulation: Standard 3D scene graphs treat objects as bounding boxes or single nodes, ignoring the specific contact geometry and part-level interactions necessary for physical stability. Introducing the Part-centric Assembly Graph (PAG) effectively bridges high-level semantics with fine-grained physical constraints.

Well-engineered procedural solver: The Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver translates topological support trees and part-to-part geometric constraints into successive feasible space clipping, sampling, and Sapien physics simulation, ensuring valid and contact-rich scene configurations.

Valuable data contribution: PARSE-10K offers 10,000 indoor scenes with dense part segmentations (averaging 17.4 parts per object, 49.9 objects per scene) and verified part-level contact graphs across 17 room types, serving as a rich benchmark for spatial intelligence.

Comprehensive validation across diverse tasks: The paper demonstrates the utility of the representation and data in both multimodal spatial reasoning (fine-tuning VLMs on visual relation and part-contact tasks) and 3D layout generation via relational diffusion.
weaknesses: Template diversity in dataset generation: Section C.2 notes that 10,000 scenes are generated based on 200 designed PAG templates created via a custom UI. Relying on 200 base graph topologies raises concerns regarding the structural diversity of the layouts, as scenes might primarily be asset-swapped variations of these 200 templates.

Unfair baseline comparison in Table 2: The evaluated commercial VLMs (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4) are tested in a zero-shot/few-shot setting, whereas 'Ours' is directly fine-tuned with LoRA on the in-domain training set. A fairer ablation would compare fine-tuning the same base model (Qwen3-VL) on standard object-level scene graph data versus fine-tuning on part-level PAG data.

Lack of standard quantitative metrics for 3D scene generation: Table 3 relies solely on a user study with 20 participants over 12 scenes. The evaluation would be considerably stronger if supplemented with standard automated layout evaluation metrics, such as object collision rates, physical stability/penetration depth, out-of-room violation rates, or FID/divergence against real indoor dataset distributions.

Heuristic surface determination: Mapping part contacts to the six bounding-box directional faces can be fragile for organic, slanted, or irregularly oriented parts, which limits generality beyond axis-aligned man-made objects.

strengths: Compelling and timely motivation: Shifting from ambiguous object-level prepositions to fine-grained, part-level geometric contacts is a meaningful step forward for embodied AI, spatial reasoning, and physically grounded 3D scene generation.

Well-formulated technical framework: The Part-centric Assembly Graph (PAG) and the Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver offer an effective coarse-to-fine constraint satisfaction formulation coupled with physical simulation (Sapien) to generate physically plausible, dense multi-object configurations.

Valuable data contribution: PARSE-10K provides 10,000 diverse indoor scenes across 17 room types with an average of ~50 objects per scene, supported by over 17,000 part-annotated assets and explicit part-level contact graphs, significantly exceeding existing CAD scene datasets in contact richness.

Comprehensive validation across multiple tasks: The utility of the representation and dataset is demonstrated on both discriminative tasks (VLM spatial reasoning, part-level contact MCQs, scene graph generation) and generative tasks (conditional 3D layout synthesis).
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison on VLM tasks: In Table 2, the 'Ours' model is obtained by LoRA fine-tuning Qwen3-VL directly on the proposed dataset, whereas the baseline models (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, Robobrain2.0, base Qwen3-VL) are evaluated zero-shot without task-specific fine-tuning. A baseline fine-tuned on object-level scene graph data (or standard visual relation datasets) would provide a clearer measure of the specific value of part-level supervision.

Limited evaluation on real-world distributions: Although Section 5.1 mentions adding some real images from COCO to the test set, the paper does not break down quantitative metrics separately between synthetic scenes and real-world images, leaving the zero-shot sim-to-real transferability of the learned part relations somewhat unclear.

Evaluation metrics for 3D scene generation: The scene generation evaluation relies primarily on visual examples and a 20-person user study comparing against InstructScene trained on 3D-FRONT. Standard quantitative layout evaluation metrics (e.g., collision rate, out-of-room violation rate, relation satisfaction rate, or Frechet Inception Distance on rendered views) should be reported to substantiate the generative claims rigorously.

Scalability and reliance on manual priors: As noted in the discussion, constructing base PAG templates still relies on manual design (200 human-designed PAGs via an authoring UI) and asset canonicalization, which currently bounds the fully automated generation of entirely novel structural topologies.

strengths: Well-motivated core insight: Current 3D scene synthesis and spatial reasoning approaches typically operate on coarse, object-level relationships that fail to specify contact surfaces and physical affordances. Framing assembly through part-level geometric relations (Part-centric Assembly Graphs, PAG) is a conceptually sound direction.

Systematic constraint-solving formulation: The coarse-to-fine spatial configuration solver (Algorithm 1) provides a clear, structured pipeline that translates semantic spatial prepositions into explicit geometric and planar constraints (e.g., face alignments, surface clipping, and collision filtering).

Dataset construction effort: Generating 10,000 physically simulated indoor scenes with part-level segmentations, canonical alignments, and extracted contact graphs provides a dense resource for spatial reasoning research.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison on spatial reasoning tasks (Table 2): The evaluation compares a fine-tuned model ('Ours', LoRA on Qwen3-VL trained directly on the proposed dataset) against zero-shot, general-purpose models (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, base Qwen3-VL). Because the tasks rely on specific coordinate serialization tokens (<|box_start|>...<|box_end|>), specific relation vocabularies, and a proprietary part ontology, the off-the-shelf baselines are at a severe disadvantage. The paper lacks a controlled ablation against other VLMs fine-tuned under comparable budgets, or evaluations on established open benchmarks (e.g., standard 3D/2D SGG benchmarks) to prove generalizability beyond in-distribution data.

Limited structural diversity due to template dependency: As detailed in Section C.2, the entire dataset of 10,000 scenes is derived from only 200 manually/semi-manually designed PAG templates across 17 room types. Averaging 50 scene instantiations per template indicates that layout topology is heavily repetitive, which limits the structural and relational diversity of PARSE-10K.

Lack of standard quantitative metrics for 3D scene generation: The 3D scene generation experiment (Section 5.2) lacks standard quantitative metrics established in prior work (such as collision/penetration volume, out-of-boundary rates, physical stability tests under gravity, or FID of rendered layouts). Relying almost exclusively on a 20-person user study over 12 scenes provides insufficient evidence to validate the generative improvements.

Ambiguity in how PAG is leveraged in the generative diffusion architecture: While Section 3 and Section 4 emphasize part-level edges, Section D.2 states that the scene generation network models pairwise relations between objects as directed edges using CLIP embeddings of coarse semantic relations (e.g., 'left of', 'below', 'supporting'). It is unclear how the fine-grained, part-to-part geometric constraints are actually ingested by the diffusion model rather than just object-level relations.

Reliance on unverified baselines and reproducibility concerns: The baseline evaluation cites and reports numbers for currently unreleased or speculative model versions (e.g., GPT-5, Claude Opus 4, Gemini 2.5), making the experimental results difficult to audit, verify, and reproduce.
